candidate_relations.reason: Sarcoidosis does not match the pruritic inverse-site lichenoid eruption or interface dermatitis of inverse lichen planus.
Deodorant avoidance produced no improvement, and the biopsy shows junction-obscuring lymphocytes supporting a lichenoid rather than allergic contact pattern.
Erythema annulare centrifugum typically has an expanding erythematous ring with trailing scale and does not represent inverse lichen planus.
Eczematous dermatitis does not capture the biopsy-supported lichenoid interface process or inverse lichen planus diagnosis.
There are no vesicles or erosions, and the reported interface histology is not dermatitis herpetiformis.
No granulomatous histology is described; the biopsy instead shows lymphocytes obscuring the dermal-epidermal junction.
The lesions lack scale, failed ketoconazole, and show lichenoid interface rather than dermatophyte-associated findings.
Seborrheic dermatitis generally produces scaly erythematous lesions and does not match the biopsy-supported inverse lichen planus.
Morphea would require clinical or histologic sclerosis, which is not described.
Nummular dermatitis is usually scaly or eczematous and does not match the lichenoid interface biopsy.
Dermatitis is compatible only as a nonspecific umbrella term and omits lichen planus and its inverse/flexural subtype.
The localized annular axillary patches and described interface inflammation do not establish lymphoma.
Absence of scale, lack of response to ketoconazole, and lichenoid interface histology argue against dermatophytosis.
The clinical course and lichenoid interface biopsy support inverse lichen planus rather than allergic contact dermatitis.
Psoriasis is a distinct diagnosis and the biopsy description favors lichenoid interface dermatitis rather than psoriasiform pathology.
Annular lichenoid dermatitis of youth is a separate lichenoid entity, whereas the benchmark is inverse lichen planus in a man in his 40s.

candidate_relations.reason: No trigger was identified, deodorant discontinuation did not help, and histology supports a lichenoid interface disorder.
The localized adult-onset annular violaceous patches and lichenoid interface biopsy do not represent atopic dermatitis.
Granuloma annulare would show dermal granulomatous or palisading inflammation rather than lymphocytes obscuring the dermal-epidermal junction.
